newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF panel calls for forex participation decontrol.
newsitem.headline: MOF panel calls for forex participation decontrol.

text.p: An advisory panel to the Finance Ministry on Thursday called for full decontrol of participation in forex deals by scrapping the current foreign exchange control rule which limits forex transactions to authorised foreign exchange banks.

This would enable participants to more easily enter and leave the currency business. This will also help banks boost their competitiveness and lead to increased liquidity of the market and activate the market.
The panel called for freer cross-border capital transactions and settlements by individuals and corporations with their overseas counterparts.
The panel will draft a report detailing the necessary changes to the foreign exchange laws, which will then be submitted as a bill to the ordinary session of parliament in January.
The main points of the report issued by the panel, a subcommittee of the Committee on Foreign Exchange and Other Transactions, are as follows:
-- scrapping existing permission and prior notification to carry out freer and speedy cross-border transactions.
-- establishing an ex post facto reporting system and continued provision of information to the market in order to comply with international agreements such as those connected to economic sanctions.
-- enabling all market participants to conduct foreign exchange business, such as sale and purchase of foreign currencies, currency future contracts, currency swaps and options.
-- Allowing firms and individuals to hold deposit accounts overseas and make settlements through multi-netting schemes without permission or prior notification.
-- Abolishing the so-called designated securities firm system and money exchanger system.

-- Abolishing limits on the foreign currencies positions of banks and other institutions at ordinary times, given the introduction of such things as the market risk regulations by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.
-- Reviewing all reports, including existing ones, in order to ascertain their necessity and merits, and drastically reduce those reporting requirements with little importance.
-- Legally requiring necessary reports to maintain the effectiveness of the ex post facto reporting system as is the norm in Western industrial countries. Violations should continue to be punished.
-- Abolishing the prior notification system and replacing it by an ex post facto reporting system in foreign direct investment.
